Q141119571.summary: Framed by a border of acanthus, this ivory plaque sets the crucified Christ at the centre of a crowded cosmic drama. Angels adore the cross between the sun and moon, figures personifying the Church and the Synagogue stand to either side, the lance-bearer and sponge-bearer flank the cross, and below the dead rise from their tombs while a foliate column carries the cross up from the world of Earth and Ocean. Made around the year 1000 for a precious liturgical book, it shows Ottonian carvers re-working the rich Carolingian crucifixion imagery of Metz.
facts: According to the French Wikipedia article, the plaque was commissioned by Adalbero II, Bishop of Metz (984–1005), as the cover of a precious liturgical book.
The titulus above Christ reads IHS NAZAREN REX IUDEORU ('Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews'), and Adam and Eve appear in contrition on the capital at the foot of the cross.
The Church (Ecclesia) is shown catching the blood from Christ's side in a vessel, while the Synagogue turns away: a pairing common in medieval crucifixion imagery.

links.label: Wikipedia (fr): Plaque de reliure dite d'Adalbéron

Q141119571.notes: The Commons file is categorised under Adalbero I of Metz (bishop 929–962), but the French Wikipedia article names Adalbero II (984–1005) and dates the plaque c. 1000; this has not been checked against the museum's own catalogue. Dimensions per Wikidata: 15.4 × 9.3 cm.

Q1281985.summary: Within an arched frame carved into the pink stone wall, Christ sits frontally with a cross-nimbus, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a book, his robe falling in flat, stylised folds. An Armenian inscription runs across the arch above his head. The figure belongs to the extraordinary programme of biblical reliefs that wraps the outside of King Gagik's palace church.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the church was built of pink volcanic tuff by the architect-monk Manuel in 915–921 as a palatine church for King Gagik I Artsruni of Vaspurakan.
Its unique importance, Wikipedia says, comes from the extensive array of bas-relief carvings of mostly biblical scenes on its external walls.
After the Armenian genocide of 1915 the church was abandoned; after restoration it reopened as a museum in 2006, and since October 2010 a cross again stands on its dome.

links.label: Wikipedia: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar

Q1281985.notes: The relief's exact position on the façade is not stated in the sources read; the inscription is not transcribed here because it could not be read reliably in the image.

vam:O130103.summary: Three crowded registers trace the Passion and its triumph. At the top, Christ hangs on the cross between the Virgin and Longinus on one side and St John and Stephaton on the other, with personifications of the Sun and Moon above; in the middle, two angels sit at the entrance of the tomb as the holy women arrive and soldiers sleep; at the bottom, Christ harrows Hell, ascends, and is shown in glory. Though much worn, the plaque is packed with narrative detail.
facts: The V&A links it to a workshop group that includes a panel in Essen and the V&A's Passion casket (216-1866); the holy women at the tomb and the Harrowing of Hell are almost identical on the two V&A pieces.
It was probably part of a book cover, perhaps of a Gospel book, and is pierced with three holes for attachment.
It came from the Webb collection (£75), and earlier from the Essingh collection in Cologne (sale 1865).

walters:44.607.summary: This small gold ring, only 1.4 cm high, has a round bezel decorated in cloisonné enamel with a cross whose arms radiate from a central medallion, apparently framing a bust; scrolls are engraved on the shoulders. The Walters identifies the image as Christ. Much of the enamel is now lost, and the figure is hard to read in the photograph.
facts: The Walters dates the ring to the 9th century and attributes it to the Byzantine Empire.
It belonged to Henry Walters and passed after his death to his widow; it was sold at Parke-Bernet in New York in 1949, when the museum bought it back.
walters:44.607.notes: Christ's presence rests on the museum's title; the worn enamel image in the available photograph cannot be clearly read as a bust of Christ. No scripture is given.

wga:zgothic/mosaics/9/8istanbu1.summary: Christ Pantocrator stands between the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist, who turn toward him in intercession for humanity on the Day of Judgment. Though the lower half has been lost, the surviving faces are among the most tender and lifelike in all Byzantine art, with soft modeling and an inward, sorrowful gentleness. It is generally thought to have been made to celebrate the recovery of Constantinople from Latin rule in 1261.
facts: 'Deësis' is Greek for 'supplication' or 'prayer' — the Virgin and the Baptist plead with Christ on behalf of mankind.
The tesserae in the faces are exceptionally small, allowing gradations of shading that approach painting.
It is often regarded as the beginning of a renaissance in Byzantine pictorial art — the so-called Palaiologan Renaissance.
The mosaic was hidden beneath plaster during the Ottoman centuries and uncovered in the 1930s by the Byzantine Institute of America under Thomas Whittemore.

commons:50399629.summary: Clothed in dazzling white within a starry mandorla, the risen Christ strides over the broken gates of Hades and pulls Adam and Eve bodily from their tombs. John the Baptist, David, Solomon and other righteous kings look on, while the personification of Death lies bound beneath his feet. It is perhaps the most dynamic image of the Resurrection in Byzantine art, the Eastern Church's preferred way of picturing Easter.
facts: The scene was painted in the funerary chapel of the monastery, making its message of resurrection directly relevant to those buried there.
The patron, the statesman and scholar Theodore Metochites, appears in a mosaic in the church offering it to Christ.
Shattered locks, keys and bolts scattered in the black abyss below Christ symbolize the destruction of death's prison.
The building, a museum from 1945, was reconverted to a mosque in 2020 and reopened for Muslim worship in May 2024.

Q108718081.summary: A slender boy in a long white robe stands among elderly teachers in a synagogue, explaining the Scriptures while they lean in to listen. Liebermann, himself Jewish, based the setting on studies made in synagogues in Amsterdam and Venice and painted Jesus as an ordinary Jewish child. Exhibited in Munich in 1879, it provoked one of the great art scandals of the century.
facts: The critic Friedrich Pecht called the boy 'the ugliest, most impertinent Jewish boy imaginable', and in January 1880 the painting was debated for two days in the Bavarian parliament.
Under the pressure, Liebermann overpainted the figure of Jesus, giving him longer, fair hair, sandals and a long white robe; studies and an early photograph show the original conception.
Liebermann later became the leading German Impressionist and president of the Prussian Academy of Arts, resigning in 1933 when the Nazis came to power.
